Inner product. An inner product is a generalization of the familiar dot product from Euclidean space to abstract vector spaces. It assigns to each pair of vectors a scalar that measures their geometric relationship. Inner products introduce notions of length, angle, and orthogonality to abstract spaces, forming the foundation of Hilbert spaces and enabling rigorous analysis in infinite dimensions. They are essential in quantum mechanics, signal processing, and functional analysis, where they provide the geometric structure underlying linear operators and spectral theory.

An inner product on a vector space assigns to each pair of vectors u and v a scalar satisfying linearity in the second argument, conjugate symmetry where the inner product of u and v equals the inner product of v and u, and positive definiteness where the inner product of v with itself is greater than zero for v not equal to zero. The dot product in n-dimensional real space is the standard inner product: the inner product of u and v equals u one v one plus u two v two and so on. This is the canonical prototype.

An inner product induces a norm equal to the square root of the inner product of v with itself. This norm measures vector length. The norm defines a metric and enables convergence and continuity arguments. Vectors u and v are orthogonal if their inner product equals zero. Orthogonal families are the analogue of perpendicular directions in Euclidean space. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states that the absolute value of the inner product of u and v is at most the norm of u times the norm of v. This fundamental inequality bounds the inner product and ensures geometric reasonableness.

The Gram-Schmidt process takes any finite set of linearly independent vectors and produces an orthonormal basis. The result consists of vectors of unit length and mutually orthogonal. This orthogonalization is crucial for numerical stability in computations. Inner products extend to spaces of functions. On the space of square-integrable functions on an interval from a to b, the inner product is the integral of f of x times g of x. This makes calculus and Fourier analysis rigorous.

A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is complete, meaning every Cauchy sequence converges. It is the primary setting for functional analysis, quantum mechanics, and spectral theory of operators.
